articleTitle: Complex-Valued Image Recovery from Multiple Measurements
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Capable of all weather day-or-night imaging, spotlight mode airborne synthetic aperture radar (SAR) is widely used for surveillance and mapping. Obtaining practically artifact- and noise-free SAR images on which practitioners can rely is imperative, and while myriad computational methods have been developed to recover SAR imagery, several challenges remain. This study develops a new recovery algorithm based in rigorous mathematical analysis to address some of these challenges. Specifically, it ensures that phase information is not lost in the recovery process, which may be important in coherent downstream processing tasks. Further, an empirical Bayesian approach is adopted to improve the robustness of the recovery as well as to provide uncertainty quantification.

articleTitle: Super-Resolution of Satellite Lidars for Forest Studies Using Diffusion Generative Models
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm for satellite lidar super-resolution using conditional Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) in the hyperheight data cube framework. The method employs a conditional reverse diffusion process to overcome challenges in long-range lidar systems, yielding high-resolution outputs from low-resolution inputs. Enhancing lidar products like canopy height models, it improves lidar-based modeling and facilitates advanced data analysis in fields such as environmental science, urban planning, and disaster management. The approach significantly enhances Earth's surface representation, creating research and application opportunities across disciplines. The framework's efficacy was validated in the Florida Everglades National Park, showcasing an enhancement from a 3m x 6m grid with 10m footprints to a 3m x 3m grid with 3m footprints, along with an increase in vertical resolution from 0.5m to 0.25m.

articleTitle: Distributing Coherence Among Phased Arrays
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: We present an approach to maintaining coherence among multiple, physically distributed phased arrays. Maintaining such coherence is essential to realizing high gain afforded by the use of multiple arrays, with the attendant improved signal-to-noise ratio that entails higher data throughput and range. The presented approach works in the context of photonically-enabled RF phased arrays that rely on upconversion of RF signals to optical domain for processing.

articleTitle: An Optically Tracked Platform for Swept Synthetic Aperture Ultrasound Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Ultrasound imaging, crucial for clinical diagnostics, is limited by diffraction, affecting resolution at depth. Swept Synthetic Aperture (SSA), counters this issue by simulating a larger aperture through lateral transducer sweeping. Incorporating an innovative calibration optimization, this study presents Optically-Tracked SSA (OT-SSA), as an unconstrained approach shown to significantly improve lateral resolution and target detectability. The paper outlines the OT-SSA frame-work, showcases image quality improvements, and discusses its role as a benchmark for future SSA technologies, including untracked methods. Specifically, we introduce a 3D printed portable motorized translation stage that facilitates data-based motion estimation using optical tracking for accuracy assessment. It signifies a step towards adaptable, clinically integrated SSA ultrasound technology.

articleTitle: A Multi-Frequency Quantitative Inversion Technique for Imaging through Obscuring Media
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: We develop a multifrequency, nonlinear quantitative inversion technique with applications to radar imaging. In particular, we perform a novel extension of a contrast source inversion algorithm, called subspace based optimization method (SOM), to its multi-frequency counterpart, called multi-frequency SOM (MFSOM). With a small angular aperture, MFSOM can range-resolve objects by introducing frequency diversity into SOM. We show that MFSOM is able to reconstruct a scatterer with improved accuracy when compared to the filtered backprojection approach. A limitation of typical radar imaging algorithms, in applications such as imaging through obscuring media, is that the range focusing of obscured scatterers is inaccurate owing to range ambiguities induced by the unknown dielectric properties of the media. Our new technique, MFSOM, is able to solve the range ambiguity problem of obscured targets by using an accurate estimate of the relative permittivity, to find the true range from the radar to a scatterer in the scene.

articleTitle: A Physics-Based Imaging and Feature Extraction Technique for Bistatic Radar Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: We present a feature extraction technique for bistatic radar imaging based on exact nonlinear anisotropic scattering representations to overcome the isotropic assumption in traditional radar imaging. We accomplish this by incorporating angle-dependent basis sets within an imaging framework. We model each unknown scatterer in a scene as the linear superposition of known bistatic pose and scale invariant bases. We define a novel anisotropic sparse imaging algorithm that replaces the isotropic assumption with our anisotropic basis set introducing an angular dependency within the imaging frame-work. We exploit a multi-resolution approach to estimate both the scale and location of the scatterer for scale invariance. Our algorithm exploits the proximal gradient descent algorithm to find the optimal mapping from the basis set to the spatial do-main. We present results for various scatterers. We validate the assumption of sparsity by comparing against its l<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-norm regularized counterpart.

articleTitle: Uncertainty in Changing Volumes of Reservoirs from Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) Mission
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: The launch of the Surface Water Ocean Topography (SWOT) satellite on December 16, 2022, signifies a groundbreaking advancement in earth's freshwater resource monitoring. Operating across Ku, C, and Ka bands, SWOT employs different retracking algorithms like Ocean, OCOG, Sea-ice, ice-2, and TFMRA. In this study, we use the first-hand datasets from SWOT mission Ku and C band post launch to estimate the uncertainty in changing volumes of lakes due to retracking algorithms. This work sheds light on the intricacies associated with utilizing SWOT data for freshwater resource assessment.

articleTitle: Adaptive Cancellation of 5G Interference
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: The wide proliferation of 5G base stations has the potential to create interference with nearby satellite receiving stations. In this paper we extend the concept of a principal component filter bank (PCFB) to a band-partitioned adaptive cancellation scheme that removes 5G interference from the received signal of a satellite ground station. By using the PCFB as an analysis tool, new insights are gained into the effects of multipath on cancellation performance.

articleTitle: Millimeter wave Multiple Input Multiple Output Inverse Synthetic Aperture Radar Images of Automotive Targets
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Prior works have demonstrated that inverse synthetic aperture radar (ISAR) images of automotive targets offer valuable information regarding the targets' shape, size, and trajectory. The images were obtained by processing single-channel wideband radar data. However, low signal-to-clutter-and-noise ratios (SCNR) limited the image quality. In this work, we examine how the image quality of automotive ISAR images can be improved by leveraging the multiple channel data available from commercially available millimeter wave automotive radars. Specifically, we exploit the multiple input multiple output (MIMO) radar signal processing framework for this purpose with three transmitting antennas and four receiving antennas using frequency-modulated continuous waveform (FMCW) at 77 GHz. We consider two MIMO configurations: time domain modulation (TDM), where the transmitters are turned on in a sequential pattern one at a time, and binary phase modulation (BPM), where all the transmitters are turned on together, and their transmissions are phase modulated. Subsequently, the data from the multiple receivers are integrated, and the corresponding ISAR images are obtained through range-Doppler processing. Finally, we compare the image quality of the resultant ISAR images obtained from these different frameworks. This work collects and processes the measurement data of multiple automotive targets using the Texas Instruments millimeter wave radar.

articleTitle: Phaseless Multi-Static Synthetic Aperture Radar Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Conventional synthetic aperture radar (SAR) relies on coherent phase information throughout the data collection process for image reconstruction. In this paper, we present a technique for phaseless SAR imaging using a multi-static configuration’ and stochastic waveforms. To reconstruct the SAR images, we employ the Wirtinger flow (WF), a non-convex optimization method. We perform numerical simulations to evaluate the performance of the WF algorithm using our proposed illumination technique. The simulation results demonstrate near-exact recovery with a limited number of resources, in terms of the number of transmitters and receivers. Hence, our proposed imaging technique has applications for realistic phaseless SAR scenarios. We compare the performance of our algorithm with that of the linear reconstruction algorithm used for phaseless radar coincidence imaging.

articleTitle: A Robust Phaseless Imaging Approach Using Reverse Kullback Leibler Divergence and Wirtinger Flow
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Phaseless imaging is a prominent field of study in many imaging modalities. In practical applications, the phaseless measurements usually contain noise and outliers, limiting the reconstruction algorithms' performance. In this paper, we study the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence (RKLD) as a robust objective function for mitigating the effects of corrupted measurements. We optimize RKLD using the state-of-the-art Wirtinger Flow (WF) algorithm for image reconstruction. Then, we numerically demonstrate the performance of RKLD using simulated coded diffraction measurements and a real optical dataset. Additionally, we compare RKLD's performance with other well-known loss functions used by the WF framework, namely, £2-intensity, Poisson, and £2-magnitude. Our simulation results demonstrate that RKLD-based optimization provides higher quality reconstructed images than the other loss functions in the presence of noise and outliers.

articleTitle: Two-Dimensional Radio-Frequency Holography Using Distributed Apertures
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: We present an approach to design two-dimensional patterns of peaks and nulls using distributed arrays of radio frequency transmitters. Simulation results validate our approach.

articleTitle: Edge-Informed Estimation of Gaussian Point Spread Functions in Convolutional Blurring Models
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: The underlying physics of imaging processes and associated instrumentation limitations mean that blurring artifacts are unavoidable in many applications such as astronomy, microscopy, radar and medical imaging. In several such imaging modalities, convolutional models are used to describe the blurring process; the observed image or function is a convolution of the true underlying image and a point spread function (PSF) which characterizes the blurring artifact. In this work, we propose and analyze a technique - based on convolutional edge detectors and Gaussian curve fitting - to approximate unknown Gaussian PSFs when the underlying true function is piecewise-smooth. For certain simple families of such functions, we show that this approximation is exponentially accurate. We also provide preliminary two dimensional extensions of this technique. These findings - confirmed by numerical simulations - demonstrate the feasibility of recovering accurate approximations to the blurring function, which serves as an important prerequisite to solving deblurring problems.

articleTitle: From Observations to Theoretical Consistency: Decoder Recovery in Coded Aperture Imaging Using Convolutional Neural Networks
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Coded aperture imaging, crucial for low-light imaging in challenging conditions, requires specific decoders for image reconstruction. Traditional image reconstruction methods can be complex and focus on reconstruction rather than learning the underlying decoder. Our work introduces a one-layer CNN network for interpretable decoder recovery, without prior knowledge of encoding or decoding arrays. Using observed detector images, the network produces reconstructed images using a learned decoder. We train our network using the MNIST dataset and report high accuracy in image reconstruction even for images with high signal to noise ratio. To validate the generalizability of the method, we show that the MNIST-trained CNN-learned decoder is able to accurately reconstruct images from the grayscale FashionMNIST dataset.

articleTitle: Eigenvector Based Block Vector Synchronization with Applications to Ptychographic Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: We consider the problem of recovering a complex vector (up to a global unimodular constant) given noisy and incomplete outer product measurements. Such problems arise when implementing distributed clock synchronization schemes, radar autofocus methods, and phaseless signal recovery. This prob-lem is known as vector synchronization and is a variant of the more common angular synchronization problem. In applications with windowed measurements and/or convolutional models - for example, phase retrieval from STFT magnitude data, the outer product measurement matrix is highly incomplete and has a block diagonal structure. We describe a vector synchronization technique which applies an eigenvector computation to blocks of this matrix followed by a block compatibility operation to piece together the final solution. We provide theoretical guarantees (in the noiseless case) and empirical simulations demonstrating the accuracy and efficiency of the method.

articleTitle: Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Sonar Ensemble Estimate Coherence
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Sonar (InSAS) measurements are noisy and typically require multiple estimates of the scene depth to constrain the vertical uncertainty (vertical resolution). Many InSAS systems sacrifice horizontal resolution for vertical resolution by utilizing spatial averaging. In previous work, we demonstrated a technique termed Seamless SAS that can form multiple observations of each image pixel, allowing us to substantially reduce the amount of spatial averaging required by supplementing it with ensembles. This paper is an extension of our previous work, focusing on furthering our theoretical understanding of the ensemble technique by analyzing the coherence between adjacent pings and synthetic aperture image strips collected by the Kraken Miniature Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Sonar (MINSAS).

articleTitle: Solopulse Approach for SAR-with-DAR
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Solopulse radar signal processing can be characterized as a frequency-wavenumber or so-called “omega-k” domain algorithm tailored specifically for digital array hardware with synthetic aperture software. Multiple data channels of a digital array radar permit image formation to commence with transmission of a single pulse, hence the moniker of “solopulse.” Solopulse is applicable at short and long ranges, and with small and large scenes. With due consideration of flight geometry and pulse repetition interval designs, coherent integration of solopulse pixel domain data from a series of single-pulse images can result in progressively enhanced cross-range resolution. Pulse-to-pulse array movement need not be linear and may be randomized. Array step sizes that exceed Nyquist bounds result in grating lobes. Solopulse can also be characterized as wideband digital beamforming where angle-steered/range-focused receive-beam sets have a high spatial-packing density. Such “regions-of-reconstruction” are obtained via spherical wave-field inversion through computationally efficient omega-k domain signal processing. Attributes of progressive resolution solopulse are explored and compared with range migration algorithm performance.

articleTitle: Synthetic Aperture Imaging Using Physically Informed Convolutional Neural Networks
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: We propose a physically informed neural network (PINN) approach to address the problem of locating scatterers using synthetic aperture radar (SAR). The proposed approach uses the physical properties of wave propagation to aid the neural network in learning to detect and localize scatterers from SAR data. This methodology is especially efficient in superresolution cases, i.e. when the scatterers are located close to each other, at distances smaller than the nominal resolution of the imaging system. Using the proposed approach, we are able to detect an a priorly unknown number of scatterers and localize them with high accuracy.

articleTitle: Instantaneous Velocity Vector Estimation Using a Single MIMO Radar Via Multi-Bounce Scattering
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) radars can estimate radial velocities of moving objects, but not their tangential velocities. In this paper, we propose to exploit multi-bounce scattering in the environment to form an effective multi-“look” synthetic aperture and enable estimation of a moving object's entire velocity vector - both tangential and radial velocities. The proposed approach enables instantaneous velocity vector estimation with a single MIMO radar, without additional sensors or assumptions about the object size. The only requirement of our approach is the existence of at least one resolvable multi-bounce path to the object from a static landmark in the environment. The approach is validated both in theory and simulation.

articleTitle: Compressed Sensing with Homodyne Detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Compressed sensing and partial Fourier sampling are two methods for accelerating MRI scans. Compressed sensing relies on the sparsity of the image in a separate domain to reduce the sampling burden and partial Fourier sampling relies on an inherent Hermitian symmetry for the same purpose. Partial Fourier with homodyne detection explicitly takes advantage of the fact that the phase of the image is low-bandwidth. Conventional combinations of these methods do not use homodyne detection; instead, the image is reconstructed by solving the same optimization algorithm as that of compressed sensing; the only difference is that a significant portion (approximately 3/8) of the samples are eliminated. In this manuscript, we reconstruct the image by solving a convex optimization problem that explicitly incorporates the low-bandwidth phase estimate of homodyne detection. We show that this method improves image quality for a given sampling burden.

articleTitle: Faster Scanning with Parallel MRI Using a Non-Rectangular Field-Of-View
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses a rectangular field-of-view (FOV) to specify the sampling pattern. The full sampling pattern is a Cartesian grid that satisfies the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem in each dimension of this FOV. Existing acceleration methods - such as partial Fourier sampling, parallel imaging, and compressed sensing - reduce the number of samples when compared to the fully sampled pattern. As human bodies are not rectangular, the rectangular FOV necessarily includes empty space. In this work, we show that the sampling pattern can be reduced with a non-rectangular FOV that better isolates empty space from subject anatomy. We show that this sampling pattern can be further accelerated in the parallel imaging setting where multiple coils are used for sensing. As the non-rectangular FOV could easily be provided by the technologist controlling the scanner, this method could readily be implemented on clinical scanners to yield faster scanning.

articleTitle: Synthetic Aperture Imaging with Neural Signal Representations
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Synthetic aperture imaging is a powerful computational imaging technique wherein a collection of low resolution measurements are computationally integrated into a single high-resolution image. This fusion step has been traditionally accomplished with pixel-based scene representations. This manuscript provides an overview of neural signal representations and describes how they can be used to enhance the synthetic aperture reconstruction pipeline.

articleTitle: Improving InSAR Accuracy for Slow Deformation and Change Detection with Lidar and GPS
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) uses two or more SAR images over the same region for mapping ground surface displacements through time. InSAR displacements are relative to a reference point due to the 2π phase ambiguity that from unwrapping, and as a result ground control points (GCPs) are often used to calibrate the displacement model and obtain absolute measurements. Errors in InSAR time-series are typically measured with respect to the reference point, but absolute errors are not currently well constrained. To develop absolute error models for InSAR, we generate Sentinel-1 InSAR time-series for Belleville, Illinois and compare time-series with Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) and Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) displacements. Both GNSS and LiDAR data showed complementary results with the InSAR measurement, demonstrating the advantages of combining InSAR with small scale LiDAR or GPS measurements to improve InSAR accuracy.

articleTitle: Deep Learning with Enforced Data Consistency
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Current deep learning methods for MRI image reconstruction handle data consistency in one of two ways: (1) add a penalty term into the loss function, or (2) add a data consis-tency layer into the network architecture. Adding a penalty to the loss function does not enforce data consistency; data inconsistent results are still often generated, which can result in erroneous reconstructions. The data consistency layer improves reconstruction quality on out-of-distribution data and largely eliminates hallucinations. However, it is too compu-tationally expensive for training with parallel imaging data. In this manuscript we explore a computationally efficient approximation to hard data consistency. We present results when adding this data consistency layer into two existing networks designed for MRI reconstruction. After retraining with the additional consistency layer, the networks show improved out-of-distribution performance and suppression of hallucinations.

articleTitle: Hybrid Strip-Line/Spotlight-Mode SAR Based on Photonic Beamforming
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) systems are widely deployed for a wide range of commercial and defense applications. Such systems are typically designed to operate in either strip-map or spotlight modes based on operational requirements. Herein, we propose a concept for a hybrid mode SAR sensor based on photonically sampled arrays, which enable multiple high-gain beams to be formed simultaneously from a single aperture, otherwise known as an imaging receiver (IMRX). This hybrid SAR utilizes concurrently-formed beams to provide the resolution benefits of spotlight mode while maintaining the full spatial-coverage advantages of strip-map SAR.

articleTitle: Elevation Mapping with Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar for Autonomous Driving
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Radar is a low cost, ubiquitous automotive sensor. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) is a class of techniques to improve azimuth resolution and sensitivity for radar. Interferometric SAR (InSAR) extracts elevation from the variations in phase measurements in SAR images. Utilizing InSAR, we show that a typical, low-resolution radar array can be used to accurately localize detections in 3D space for human-scale autonomous driving environments. We form a point cloud of detailed structures for complex automotive scenes by combining In-SAR with additional signal processing operations. This technique is feasible for real-time processing with low latency.

articleTitle: Detection and Characterization of Drones in Urban Environments with Synthetic Aperture Radar Images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: This work examines synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging of a commercial drone in an artificial urban environment. We used a 10 GHz frequency modulated continuous wave (FMCW) SAR imaging system with a 1.5 GHz bandwidth inside an electromagnetic anechoic chamber to generate SAR images for target detection and characterization. We considered combinations of two ranges, two cross-ranges, and five elevation angles. We constructed a brick wall inside the anechoic chamber and behind the drone to simulate the scenario of a drone flying very close to structures in an urban environment. From the initial SAR imaging and simulation results, we found that SAR imaging can detect and distinguish different drone orientations in an artificial urban environment.

articleTitle: Wall Localization in a Water Tank Using a Cooperative Source of Opportunity
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Model-based underwater acoustic localization in confined spaces like water tanks typically depend on the geometry. This paper investigates the problem of water tank wall localization using an acoustic source of opportunity that may not offer sufficient bandwidth for time-of-arrival-based methods to perform satisfactorily. We propose that in these scenarios, approximate time-of-arrival-based methods are used followed by a ray-based differentiable model using a gradient-based optimization to obtain a more accurate estimate. We demon-strate the successful operation of the algorithm on data ob-tained from a tank simulator, whose parameters are adjusted to those of the Scripps Ocean Atmosphere Research Simula-tor (SOARS).

articleTitle: Towards Full Field-of-View Fourier Ptychography for Extreme Ultraviolet Microscope
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: We evaluate various Fourier ptychographic microscopy (FPM) reconstruction algorithms using both simulated and experimental data acquired from an Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV, 13.5 nm wavelength) microscope. We specifically focus on the algorithms' ability to robustly address field-dependent aberrations, which enables increased spatial resolution and quantitative phase imaging across an expanded field of view. We systematically compare the algorithms' performance under aberrations for a single zoneplate imaging system, utilizing Fourier Ring Correlation (FRC) as a systematic metric for assessing reconstruction quality. Furthermore, we explore the impact of systematic errors on the reconstruction of experimental data, aiming to increase the effective field of view by 25-fold, from the nominal 5x5 um<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> diffraction-limited area. Additionally, our evaluation incorporates innovative FPM-adjacent methodologies, including the Angular Ptychographic Imaging with Closed-form method (APIC), for reconstructing EUV images.

articleTitle: Ptychographic Synthetic Aperture Imaging with Intensity-Only Measurements
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Ptychography has emerged as a transformative coherent diffraction imaging technique for both fundamental and applied sciences. Here we discuss a coded ptychography technique that achieves an imaging throughput order of magnitude greater than conventional microscopy approaches. In this platform, we translate the samples across the disorder-engineered surfaces for lensless diffraction data acquisition. The engineered surface can be made by smearing a monolayer of blood on top of the image sensor. The entire system can be built using a modified Blu-ray player, where the 405 nm laser from the optical pickup head can be used as a coherent light source for sample illumination. By tracking the phase wraps of the recovered images, we report the direct observation of bacterial growth in a 1-s interval at a 120 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> area, with a phase sensitivity like that obtained from interferometric measurements. We also characterize cell growth via longitudinal dry mass measurement and perform rapid bacterial detection at low concentrations. The combination of high phase sensitivity, high spatiotemporal resolution, and ultra-large field of view is unique among existing microscopy techniques. We will also discuss the several extensions of the coded ptychography technique, including synthetic aperture ptychography, polarimetric coded ptychography, and depth-multiplexed ptychographic microscopy, thereby expanding its applicability in different fields.

articleTitle: Distributed Antenna Arrays for Simultaneous Nulling and Sectorized Jamming
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: This paper investigates distributed beamforming networks composed of multiple groups of mobile transmitters. The goal is to jointly optimize the beamforming weights and the orientation angles of the groups to maximize the radiated power over an angular sector containing an adversary while placing a null towards the client in order to improve the communication security of the client. The antennas in each group may be closely spaced forming a compact array and mutual coupling effects are fully included. The joint optimization problem is computationally difficult so several related optimization problems are considered that lead to simpler solutions. The approach is frequency-agnostic but is particularly appealing for low frequencies where the wavelength is relatively large and compact arrays simplify positioning and synchronization in the network. Numerical simulations are presented that validate the effectiveness of the methods.

articleTitle: Triangular Direction of Arrival Architecture for Synthetic Aperture Radiometers
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Directions of Arrival (DoA) with sparse radiometer arrays achieve angular resolution through Time Difference of Arrival (TDoA) between those sparse elements. A thinly populated array of apertures has a limit that is set by bandwidth and how large a separation between elements is allowable. Bandwidths used by radiometers to support temperature sensitivity can profitably offer spatial resolution in thermographic imaging by an array of radiometers. This work describes how this may be achieved.

articleTitle: Laboratory-Based Reference Channels for Millimeter-Wave Wireless Device Measurements
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Industrial and consumer wireless devices increasingly make use of millimeter-wave (mmWave) frequencies to meet requirements for bandwidth and latency. The complex propagation environment and design of phased-array antennas pose a dual challenge to mmWave implementation. We have developed a mmWave testbed for industrial internet-of-things devices, which implements realistic mmWave channels in a repeatable and enclosed environment. Synthetic-aperture techniques are used to capture real-world channel information, replicate key channel features within our testbed, and, ultimately, will provide a traceable reference measurement against which mmWave devices may be compared. In this paper, an overview of the testbed is presented, and initial measurement results are provided for an “exemplar” industrial mmWave channel.

articleTitle: Multi-Modal Extreme-Ultraviolet Reflectometer: Solving Inverse Problems in Nanostructure Metrology
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Conference on Computational Imaging Using Synthetic Apertures (CISA)
abstract: Coherent extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) light offers researchers chemical specificity and spatial resolution that is ideal for nanostructure metrology. Combining appropriate physical forward models that capture EUV light-sample interactions and propagation, the experimental data, and optimization routines, one can measure important parameters of nanostructured samples. In this paper, we discuss a unique instrument, designed to characterize the multilayer composition, geometry, topography, and interface quality of various nanostructured samples. We utilize the advantage of coherent EUV light and demonstrate three modes of characterizations, including reflectometry, scatterometry, and coherent diffractive imaging (CDI) reflectometry.
